paragraphs.text: A loose [Liu Bao](liu-bao:definition) made in 1990 from leaf grown in Cangwu County, which came to us through the Guangzhou tea trade. That route is an old one. In the [river trade](liu-bao:nanyang-trade), the tea went by boat down to Wuzhou and on to Guangzhou, then out by sea to the Chinese miners and labourers of Southeast Asia.

Cangwu is a county under [Wuzhou](guangxi:wuzhou-and-cangwu), in eastern Guangxi, and Liubao town, which gave the tea its name, lies inside it. The area is warm and wet, with acidic soils. The trade links that [steady damp warmth](guangxi:land-and-climate) to the slow ageing of Liu Bao, because the microbes that shape a dark tea thrive in it.

Like every dark tea, the leaf was piled after it was made so that warmth, moisture and microbes could darken and soften it, and then it was packed to age. Thirty-six years on, it is well past the ten years after which the trade counts a Liu Bao as [aged](liu-bao:age-aged). The way it was stored has shaped it as much as the years have.

brewing.text: Liu Bao takes very hot or boiling water, because its leaf is dense and gives up its depth slowly. Rinse it once or twice and pour the rinse away. Use about 5 to 8 grams to 100 ml, start with steeps of five to fifteen seconds and add a few seconds each round; a good Liu Bao gives ten cups or more.

notice.text: A deep red, thick cup with woody, herbal and betel nut notes; tea several decades old is often described with ginseng and camphor.
